newsitem.title: USA: Resolution of tobacco issues may still take years.
newsitem.headline: Resolution of tobacco issues may still take years.

text.p: Although the tobacco industry was dealt a major blow Friday when a U.S. District Court judge ruled that the Food and Administration (FDA) can regulate sales and labeling on cigarettes, industry and legal experts said many more dollars will be spent by both sides in an appeals process that could take years.
In a statement after the ruling, the U.S. tobacco industry renewed its call for a legislative resolution of the tobacco controversy.

The industry statement also noted that Judge William Osteen ruled that the FDA cannot restrict the advertising and promotion of tobacco products, and issued an injunction against additional implementation of new regulations.

People familiar with the dispute said both the industry and the FDA are talking about taking the case to the U.S. Court of Appeals. One source said that depending on the outcome there, the case could eventually go the U.S. Supreme Court which is a very lengthy process.

An attorney not involved in tobacco cases noted that the industry has fought long and hard against having the nicotine in tobacco declared a drug, and thus lost a key point in Friday's ruling. The attorney asked that he not be identified.

The ruling came as the industry continued under assault from a variety of sources, including suits by individual smokers and the attorneys general of 23 states suing the industry over the costs of tobacco-realted disease.

"It doesn't help their predicament at the bargaining table," said Mary Aronson of Aronson Washington Research, referring to the recent talks between the industry and anti-smoking forces. "If anything it helps the other side."
As for lawsuits by individual smokers or their families, Aronson said Osteen's ruling would not have much bearing.

In the talks the industry is bargaining with plaintiffs' lawyers, attorneys general and the public health community. Several sources said the talks will probably resume in the latter part of this week. One source noted that because the decision Friday was mixed, it will just make the talks that much more complicated as each side tries to refine its position.

An editorial published in the Spring 1997 issue of the British Medical Association's journal Tobacco Control focused on the situation in the United States and said that public health interests must make sure that any settlement or legislative solution is part of a comprehensive package of "truly effective tobacco policies."

The editorial among other things called for a total ban on tobacco advertising and promotion; funding for programs and research in tobacco control; funding for a large national, media-led anti-tobacco campaign and cessation assistance for addicted smokers. Dr David Burns of the University of California San Diego Medical Center was lead author of the editorial, which was also signed by seven colleagues.
Tobacco stocks fell Friday, including Philip Morris Cos Inc which declined 2-1/8 to 39-1/2 and RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp which skidded 2-3/4 to 28-7/8.
